guidance.when: Always apply before classifying assets. Use only jurisdictions already declared allowable in the facts or public prior.
guidance.procedure: Enumerate every eligible asset-citation alternative, not a final portfolio. Federal section 522(d) and applicable state/local exemptions are alternative schemes under 11 U.S.C. § 522(b); joint debtors cannot split schemes. Arizona and Illinois expressly prohibit section 522(d); do not infer another state's opt-out. For EV, assess each asset-citation pair independently, preserve the exact asset name/value and citation, and use null only when this bank publishes an operator for that citation. Aggregate caps remain legal constraints even though the task does not allocate them across assets. N is 1 or 2 debtors; spouse multiplication applies only where the supplied text supports separate exemptions.
guidance.avoid_when: Do not recompute domicile or allowable jurisdictions, mix elected schemes into one portfolio, add claims together, infer eligibility from an operator, or treat an aggregate ceiling as a per-item entitlement.

guidance.when: Use only when the federal section 522(d) scheme is allowable: residence or burial plot (d)(1); one motor vehicle (d)(2); enumerated personal or household items (d)(3); personal/family jewelry (d)(4); any property wildcard (d)(5); trade tools/books/implements (d)(6); professionally prescribed health aids (d)(9).
guidance.procedure: Section 522(m) gives each joint debtor a separate exemption, subject to the common scheme election. The formulas combine equal jointly owned interests. For (d)(3), the routine is for one particular item; a qualifying collection instead requires inline min(V,14875*N), while no individual item may exceed 700 per debtor. The (d)(5) routine states the maximum independent alternative: 1475 plus 13950 of wholly unused (d)(1), per debtor. If less (d)(1) remains unused, calculate the supported numeric ceiling inline. Health aids have no dollar ceiling, so use inline unlimited.
guidance.avoid_when: Do not use section 522(d) for Arizona or Illinois residents, use (d)(3) for unlisted property, multiply a single debtor's cap merely because property is jointly held, or call the (d)(5) routine when the full unused-homestead amount is unavailable under the intended alternative.

guidance.when: Use only for allowable Arizona law. Consider the occupied homestead or protected proceeds, residual household property, specifically enumerated personal items, every motor vehicle as an independent asset-law alternative, prescribed prostheses, a qualifying account, and qualifying business or farm property.
guidance.procedure: Classify under Arizona law before applying a ceiling. Output Ariz. Rev. Stat. § 33-1125(8) for each qualifying motor vehicle even when the estate contains more than one, because this task reports alternatives rather than a simultaneous election. Ariz. Rev. Stat. § 33-1125(4) applies only when the facts identify an engagement ring or wedding ring; a ring or other jewelry without that character receives no claim under that citation. Ariz. Rev. Stat. § 33-1123 is limited to personally used household property not specifically prescribed elsewhere. Ariz. Rev. Stat. § 33-1121 permits spouses to combine article exemptions using N, but Ariz. Rev. Stat. § 33-1101(A) permits only one 400000 homestead for a married couple. Protected proceeds under Ariz. Rev. Stat. § 33-1101(C) remain subject to that ceiling and the stated time and replacement-homestead conditions. Use inline unlimited for eligible property under Ariz. Rev. Stat. § 33-1125(9) or Ariz. Rev. Stat. § 33-1125(11).
guidance.avoid_when: Do not cite federal law or another state's law, suppress a qualifying vehicle because another vehicle is present, infer engagement or wedding status merely from the word ring, double the homestead, use Ariz. Rev. Stat. § 33-1123 for property specifically prescribed elsewhere, or treat a personal commuting vehicle as a trade tool.

guidance.when: Use only for allowable Illinois law. For personal, nonbusiness property, consider the residual exemption in 735 Ill. Comp. Stat. 5/12-1001(b). Also consider the specific provisions for an occupied residence or protected proceeds, necessary apparel and listed materials, a motor vehicle, trade implements or books, and prescribed health aids.
guidance.procedure: Classify before valuing. For every personal-use item, test 735 Ill. Comp. Stat. 5/12-1001(b), including an ordinary household item, firearm, or motor vehicle. A qualifying motor vehicle has two independent alternatives: 735 Ill. Comp. Stat. 5/12-1001(b) and 735 Ill. Comp. Stat. 5/12-1001(c); output both full citations. Under the supplied benchmark treatment, the residual ceiling is 4000*N, while the vehicle ceiling is 2400 without multiplying by N. Section 735 Ill. Comp. Stat. 5/12-901 uses 15000*N for the stipulated equal interests, and qualifying proceeds under 735 Ill. Comp. Stat. 5/12-906 use 15000*N for one year. Eligible property under 735 Ill. Comp. Stat. 5/12-1001(a) or 735 Ill. Comp. Stat. 5/12-1001(e) has no dollar ceiling and requires inline unlimited.
guidance.avoid_when: Do not abbreviate an Illinois citation, substitute the motor-vehicle provision for the residual alternative, classify an ordinary appliance as a trade tool without business facts, multiply the 2400 motor-vehicle ceiling by N, apply these personal-property provisions to business property, or combine independently reported alternatives into one recovery.

guidance.when: Use for allowable Oregon law. Classify under the exact categories in 18.345, the personal-property residual, one qualifying firearm per person, or the occupied homestead and qualifying proceeds.
guidance.procedure: For joint household judgment debtors, only 18.345(1)(a),(b),(c),(d),(p) are separately claimable and combinable, hence their N formulas; (e),(f),(h) are not doubled by 18.345(3). For 18.345(1)(e), write inline min(V,1000) for animals/poultry but unlimited for eligible 60-day food. For (f), write min(V,3000) for household goods and unlimited for eligible 60-day provisions or fuel. Prescribed health aids use unlimited. The homestead routine uses the special combined 50000 ceiling for two household debtors; the same ceiling governs qualifying one-year proceeds intended for another homestead.
guidance.avoid_when: Do not double categories omitted from 18.345(3), disregard necessity or habitual-earnings requirements for tools, claim more than one qualifying firearm per person, or use the two-debtor homestead ceiling unless both household members' interests are exposed.

guidance.when: Use for allowable Pennsylvania law. Section 8123 reaches property generally; section 8124 separately covers wearing apparel, Bibles and school books, qualifying family or seamstress sewing machines, and qualifying military uniforms and accoutrements.
guidance.procedure: Enumerate section 8123 along with any applicable specific citation because it is expressly additional. Each spouse has a separate 300 exemption. Use inline unlimited for eligible 8124(a)(1)-(4), because those provisions state no dollar ceiling.
guidance.avoid_when: Do not treat unlimited as eliminating the stated ownership, occupation, use, sale-or-hire, or military-status conditions; do not combine independent alternatives into a final portfolio.

guidance.when: Use for allowable Wisconsin law: burial property; business/farm assets or the alternative closely held business interest; listed consumer goods; motor vehicles; personal nonbusiness depository accounts; and an occupied homestead or protected proceeds.
guidance.procedure: Section 815.18(8) gives each spouse one capped exemption that may be combined, reflected by N. Business-interest paragraph (b)(2) is available only if (b)(1) is not claimed. Consumer goods have a 12000 aggregate cap per spouse. Motor vehicles have a 4000 base per spouse plus unused consumer-goods capacity; the routine gives the maximum independent ceiling of 16000 per spouse. If less consumer capacity remains, calculate a supported numeric expression inline. Burial property has no dollar ceiling and uses inline unlimited. Section 815.20 expressly allows each spouse 75000; protected sale proceeds keep that ceiling for two years while intended for another homestead.
guidance.avoid_when: Do not claim both business alternatives, use a business account under (k), treat the transferred consumer-goods amount as available twice in a portfolio, classify a motor vehicle under the general consumer-goods residual instead of (g), or ignore occupancy, proceeds-intent, lien, tax, aggregate, or primary-use conditions.

guidance.avoid_when: Do not claim both business alternatives, use a business account under (k), treat the transferred consumer-goods amount as available twice in a portfolio, classify a motor vehicle under the general consumer-goods residual instead of (g), or ignore occupancy, proceeds-intent, lien, tax, aggregate, or primary-use conditions.

guidance.when: Use only for allowable Illinois law. For personal, nonbusiness property, consider the residual exemption in 735 Ill. Comp. Stat. 5/12-1001(b). Also consider the specific provisions for an occupied residence or protected proceeds, necessary apparel and listed materials, a motor vehicle, trade implements or books, and prescribed health aids.
guidance.procedure: Classify before valuing. For every personal-use item, test 735 Ill. Comp. Stat. 5/12-1001(b), including an ordinary household item, firearm, or motor vehicle. A qualifying motor vehicle has two independent alternatives: 735 Ill. Comp. Stat. 5/12-1001(b) and 735 Ill. Comp. Stat. 5/12-1001(c); output both full citations. Apply subsection (c) only when the property itself is a motor vehicle. A word such as automatic or semi-automatic describing how a firearm or appliance operates does not make that property a motor vehicle; such personal property remains under subsection (b), not subsection (c). Under the supplied benchmark treatment, the residual ceiling is 4000*N, while the vehicle ceiling is 2400 without multiplying by N. Section 735 Ill. Comp. Stat. 5/12-901 uses 15000*N for the stipulated equal interests, and qualifying proceeds under 735 Ill. Comp. Stat. 5/12-906 use 15000*N for one year. Eligible property under 735 Ill. Comp. Stat. 5/12-1001(a) or 735 Ill. Comp. Stat. 5/12-1001(e) has no dollar ceiling and requires inline unlimited.
guidance.avoid_when: Do not abbreviate an Illinois citation, substitute the motor-vehicle provision for the residual alternative, apply subsection (c) to a firearm or other nonvehicle merely because its description contains automatic or semi-automatic, classify an ordinary appliance as a trade tool without business facts, multiply the 2400 motor-vehicle ceiling by N, apply these personal-property provisions to business property, or combine independently reported alternatives into one recovery.

operations.rationale: The rejected broad three-skill revision improved current cases but regressed earlier EV outputs through cross-jurisdiction and extra-claim errors. This narrower repair preserves the parent Illinois routine and addresses the observed case-28 EV false claim: the executor mistook a firearm's semi-automatic descriptor for motor-vehicle eligibility under subsection (c), although the same asset belongs under the personal-property residual subsection (b).
